title: A contact center move: a contract type, a borrowed engineer, a late vendor and a cost forecast

brief.situation: You are the project manager for the City of Alder Bay, a fictional city, moving its 311 contact center to the new Harbor Street building. The project is predictive: 10 weeks from Monday 5 July 2027 and 300 thousand dollars, with a 10 thousand dollar contingency reserve. The IT department lends you its network engineer; Ridgeline Networks, a fictional vendor, installs the network and phones under contract.
handover: Sponsor: Marcus Hale, deputy city manager, who holds the management reserve. IT director: Joan Whitaker. 311 supervisors run the floor.
Planned value is 30 thousand dollars a week; the dashboard shows PV, EV, AC, SPI, CPI and the estimate at completion.
howItWorks: The dashboard shows the objective, baseline and reserves, the work packages, earned value against plan, the open issues, the people and the milestones.
Move the project on a week at a time. Decisions come to you as they arise; before them you can read the resource plan or the vendor's contract.
At go-live you close the project and write a short note.

then.log: The migration vendor's fixed price carries a 40% premium for the unknown data quality.
Cost-plus with no ceiling: the vendor's hours on data cleansing keep growing.
Data cleansing runs over its estimate; the not-to-exceed ceiling caps it.
A vendor engineer backfills for a week.
No network engineer: cabling sign-off and phone configuration wait.
Ridgeline Networks reports 40% of the cabling against a 70% milestone.
Ridgeline works to its recovery plan: a second crew on weekends, at its own cost under the contract.
Terminated mid-installation: a new vendor must be found and the half-done cabling inspected.

effects.log: End of week 1: the data migration contract.
End of week 3: a call from the IT director.
End of week 5: the network milestone.

contractPrompt.title: End of week 1: which contract for the CRM data migration?
contractPrompt.context: Nobody knows how clean the legacy CRM's 400,000 records are; the vendor's estimate is 6 to 14 days of cleansing. The fit-out, a clearly specified job, is already under a fixed-price contract.

choices.label: Time and materials with a not-to-exceed ceiling and weekly hours reports: the scope is uncertain, so the city takes the risk but caps it

effects.log: Signed: time and materials, ceiling 40 thousand dollars, weekly reports.

choices.feedback: Uncertain scope fits time and materials or cost-reimbursable work; a not-to-exceed ceiling limits the buyer's risk.

choices.label: Fixed price, so the vendor carries the risk

effects.log: The vendor prices the uncertainty in.

choices.feedback: A fixed price on uncertain scope buys a risk premium, or invites change orders later.

choices.label: Cost plus a fee, with no ceiling: the vendor knows best
choices.feedback: Cost-reimbursable work puts the risk on the buyer; without a ceiling or reporting, nothing limits it.

resPrompt.title: End of week 3: the IT director wants the network engineer back
resPrompt.context: The IT director: "A server failure at the water plant needs Dana for two weeks, starting Monday." Dana is on the move's critical path in weeks 3 to 6.

choices.label: Meet the IT director with the critical path and the resource plan: agree to lend Dana for three days, and backfill the rest with a vendor engineer (4 thousand dollars); go to the sponsor only if you cannot agree

effects.log: Agreed: Dana goes for three days; a vendor engineer covers the rest.

choices.feedback: Resource conflicts in a matrix organization are negotiated with the functional manager using the plan, with escalation as the plan says.

choices.label: Ask the sponsor to overrule the IT director

effects.log: The sponsor overrules IT; Dana stays.

choices.feedback: Escalating first skips the negotiation the plan asks for and costs the relationship with the functional manager.

choices.label: Let Dana go for two weeks and hope the network work catches up

effects.log: Dana leaves the project for two weeks.

choices.feedback: Giving up a critical-path resource without analysis or a backfill moves the delay onto the project.

vendorPrompt.title: End of week 5: the network vendor missed its milestone
vendorPrompt.context: Ridgeline Networks has finished 40% of the cabling against a 70% milestone; its project lead blames a crew shortage. Ridgeline's next invoice arrives Monday.

choices.label: Evaluate the performance against the contract's milestones, issue the cure notice under clause 9, require a recovery plan at Ridgeline's cost, and record the evaluation

effects.log: Cure notice issued; Ridgeline presents a weekend-crew recovery plan.

choices.feedback: Vendor performance is evaluated against the contract's criteria, and the contract's remedies are invoked in their order.

choices.label: Terminate the contract now and rebid
choices.feedback: Termination before the contract's cure step costs time, money and possibly a dispute.

choices.label: Pay the invoice and wait; they say they will catch up
choices.feedback: Paying without a performance review gives up the contract's leverage.

financePrompt.title: End of week 7: the cost forecast
financePrompt.context: CPI is {cpi|2dp}; the estimate at completion (BAC / CPI) is about {round(300 / cpi)} thousand dollars against a 300 thousand budget. The contingency reserve is spent. The city's finance office releases money quarterly; the sponsor holds a management reserve.

choices.label: Report the forecast with its causes and ask the sponsor, through change control, for 15 thousand dollars of management reserve

effects.log: The sponsor approves 15 thousand dollars of management reserve; the cost baseline is updated.

choices.feedback: Project finances are forecast from performance; an overrun is reported with its cause and funded through the sponsor's reserve and change control.

choices.label: Charge the overrun to next quarter's operating budget so the project reports on budget

effects.log: The overrun moves to an operating budget.

choices.feedback: Moving project cost to another budget misreports the project's finances.

choices.label: Cut agent training from four days to one to stay within the budget

effects.log: Training cut to one day; the supervisors were not asked.

choices.feedback: Cutting scope to hide a cost variance trades a reported overrun for an unready contact center.

reflection.question: Write the close-out note for the sponsor: the contract type you chose and why, how the resource conflict and the vendor were handled, and how the project's finances were forecast and funded.

parts.label: Contract and vendor
parts.criteria: Chooses time and materials with a ceiling for uncertain scope and says why; evaluates Ridgeline against the contract and uses its cure step.
parts.modelAnswer: The migration's scope was unknown, so time and materials with a 40 thousand dollar ceiling: the city carried the risk but capped it. Ridgeline missed its 70% milestone; we evaluated it against the contract and issued a cure notice, and its recovery plan brought the network in by week 7.

parts.label: Resources and finances
parts.criteria: Negotiates the critical-path resource with the functional manager before escalating; forecasts EAC from CPI and funds the overrun through the sponsor's reserve and change control.
parts.modelAnswer: We agreed three days for Dana and a vendor backfill with the IT director. At week 7 the forecast was above budget; we reported it and the sponsor approved 15 thousand dollars of management reserve through change control.

scoring.modelReasoning: Contract type follows scope certainty: a clearly specified fit-out suits a fixed price; a migration whose data quality nobody knows suits time and materials with a not-to-exceed ceiling, so the buyer carries a capped risk instead of paying a premium. In a matrix organization a critical-path resource conflict is negotiated with the functional manager using the plan before it goes to the sponsor. A vendor that misses a milestone is evaluated against the contract and the contract's remedies are used in their order: cure notice and recovery plan before termination. Finances are forecast from performance (EAC = BAC / CPI); an overrun is reported with its cause and funded from the sponsor's management reserve through change control, not hidden or cut from scope.
